transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Lena Hart (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Janelle Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - AtlasIQ), Evan Brooks (Platform), Maria Soto (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
- Goal: stress Redwood with long session context + bursts of high TPS and observe streaming behavior, KV cache eviction, and graceful fallback options.
- Actions: benchmark run, security docs, pilot plan.

[00:00] Lena Hart: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm lena from Redwood, i own this account.
[00:06] Priya Nair: hi lena, priya here, thanks. Evan and Maria are on as well.
[00:10] Evan Brooks: yeah thanks. we're hoping to see how you handle really long histories — think 200k tokens plus — and also sudden spikes, like 2–3k concurrent requests for short windows.
[00:20] Diego Morales: cool, that's exactly what we planned to walk through. we'll show API examples, a console live view, and then some Optimize tips. quick note, some transcriptions might flip product names — "Redwood Optimize" might show as "Redwood Optimaise" in the notes.
[00:32] Maria Soto: perfect. also we have strict network egress rules. if we do on-prem, need to understand VPC peering and KMS flow.

[05:10] Diego Morales: starting with long context: our runtime supports KV cache streaming so you don't resend full history every time. for 200k tokens we suggest prefix caching with the session pinned to the same shard. when the session grows beyond the active KV window we do incremental truncation — you will see some context erosion behavior, which is by design to keep latency stable.
[05:45] Evan Brooks: what does "erosion" look like? is it sudden or gradual?
[05:50] Janelle Park: mostly gradual; we evict least-recently-used kv entries at chunk boundaries. if you have repeated prefixes we can do aggressive prefix caching to avoid re-computation. in a stress scenario you might see the model drop older instructions first, so put critical state in pinned metadata.
[06:28] Priya Nair: hmm okay. any differences between hosted and private for this?
[06:35] Diego Morales: private gives you control over instance sizing and longer-lived cache residency because you control eviction policies. hosted is tuned to balance multi-tenant throughput so the eviction window can be shorter under heavy load.

[12:00] Lena Hart: switching to streaming backpressure — we'll simulate a token surge where many concurrent streams exceed the batcher's comfortable size.
[12:18] Diego Morales: demo note: when streaming buffers back up we apply two mechanisms: graceful partial flush (send current tokens and continue) and selective shedding (shift some low-priority requests to a fallback model or queue). the goal is to avoid hard timeouts for high-priority sessions.
[12:49] Evan Brooks: will clients see increased latency or timeouts?
[12:52] Diego Morales: short answer: some latency increase is expected during surges. timeouts are avoided by policy — e.g., we prefer to route to a smaller, cheaper model to keep response streaming, or return interim partial results with an indicator that finalization is pending.
[13:24] Maria Soto: do you expose these policies in the console? we need visibility for SRE.
[13:30] Janelle Park: yes, Console shows per-route SLOs, current queue length, and token backlog. you can trigger an automatic fallback in the routing policy or manual failover. we also surface which model variant served the last N requests.

[18:05] Priya Nair: can we set different priorities per route? some of our traffic is low-priority telemetry, others are customer-facing chat.
[18:12] Diego Morales: absolutely — routing rules support priority weights, region preferences, and fallback chains. for example, you can pin high-priority routes to Dedicated capacity and let low-priority land on hosted or a quantized variant.

[24:40] Evan Brooks: curious about real numbers: what's the tail latency for 3k TPS with 200k-context?
[24:46] Diego Morales: depends on model size and quantization. rough numbers: with a 7B quantized model on a multi-GPU pod we see p95 generation latencies around 350–700 ms per token under steady-state. but with extremely long KV lookups (200k context) the first few tokens may be higher — could spike to 1.5–2s if the cache is cold.
[25:15] Priya Nair: that cache cold start is concerning; can we pre-warm?
[25:20] Janelle Park: yes — pre-warm by pinning sessions to pods, or push a warm prefix using the pre-load API. Optimize can recommend warm-up sizes given your trace.

[30:10] Maria Soto: we worry about streaming timeouts in our mobile clients; many use a 10s idle timeout. How do you handle partial streams?
[30:18] Diego Morales: we surface keep-alive heartbeats and chunked partial responses. clients can treat a partial chunk as usable. if idle time exceeds your client timeout we recommend the client maintain a websocket or re-request with the token window — but we can also configure shorter micro-chunks to avoid idle gaps.

[35:40] Evan Brooks: what happens when the KV cache gets evicted mid-session and the model forgets an earlier instruction? is there any auto-synthesis?
[35:46] Diego Morales: we provide a TTL-based checkpointing mechanism: you can snapshot important state to the customer-managed store and rehydrate on eviction. plus Optimize suggests which tokens to keep (salience scoring). note: transcriptions sometimes garble "checkpoint" as "check point" ; ignore minor auto captions.

[42:10] Lena Hart: quick Demo: live console view — (screen share) — showing route metrics, token backlog chart, and a playback of a simulated surge.
[42:25] Janelle Park: you can see the backlog spike at t+00:20 and the system applies selective shedding — those low priority requests are rerouted to the quantized-3b variant, the high priority stayed on the reserved pod.
[42:50] Evan Brooks: the timeline labels are helpful. do you emit event logs for each reroute? we need them for auditing.
[42:56] Janelle Park: yes — audit logs include reroute reason, model id, pod id, and latency impact. they can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[49:05] Priya Nair: security questions: for private deployment, how does KMS flow work? we use HSM-backed keys.
[49:12] Diego Morales: for private we integrate with your KMS/HSM via customer-managed key rotations; secrets never transit our control plane in plaintext. note that some transcriptions may show KMS as "K-M-S" or "KMS" inconsistently.

[53:30] Evan Brooks: what SLOs do you guarantee for Dedicated?
[53:35] Lena Hart: Dedicated has an SLA for pod availability and best-effort latency targets — we publish p99 targets per model family in the contract; exact numbers are part of the reserved capacity docs. we'll share the SLA excerpt in the follow-up.

[58:00] Maria Soto: can you show Optimize's concrete suggestion example for batching?
[58:06] Janelle Park: sure — Optimize looked at your sample trace and suggested batching window of 12–25ms with a max batch size of 256 for a 7B quantized model to balance latency and cost. for long contexts it also recommended prefix-level caching and a fallback policy that drops non-essential tokens first.

[63:20] Evan Brooks: any known gotchas with websocket streaming vs server-sent events?
[63:26] Diego Morales: websockets give persistent channels and simpler keep-alive; SSE is fine but some proxies may buffer SSE. also, some mobile carriers kill websockets after idle period — so we recommend heartbeats at 15s intervals.

[67:45] Priya Nair: recap?
[67:48] Lena Hart: recap: 1) we'll run an on-prem pilot simulating 3k TPS bursts with long contexts; 2) we will send benchmark & cost model; 3) security docs + SLA excerpt; 4) Diego will run the sim and post logs; 5) follow-up meeting to review pilot results week of Aug 16.
[68:10] Priya Nair: sounds good. please include a sample request shape and config for our SREs.
[68:18] Lena Hart: will do. thanks everyone.
[68:22] Evan Brooks: thanks, bye.
[68:24] Maria Soto: bye.
